title: A day of effort
hookLine: does effort have to feel grim? one answer, and a neighbor's verse
tomorrow: what if patience isn't the same as waiting quietly?

cards: Every so often you lose track of time doing something hard: a puzzle, a drawing, a long run where your legs stop complaining. Afterward you're tired and somehow lighter. Some people call it being in the zone.
The Buddhist word for effort, viriya, came up two days ago. Today's question is how it's supposed to feel. Grim?

teach.b: The Buddhist sources lean toward joy. In the factors of awakening, energy sits right beside rapture, and one discourse says that when a mind is sluggish, it's investigation, energy and joy that lift it.
Shantideva, the Mahayana teacher, goes further in his guide to the bodhisattva's way.

teach.h: EFFORT IS DELIGHT IN THE GOOD.
teach.b: He defines effort as delight in the good. Its enemy is laziness, and he counts more than lying around as laziness: being drawn to petty things, and putting yourself down. This is one place Buddhists have neighbors.
The Qur'an, in Pickthall's translation, says: "And that man hath only that for which he maketh effort, And that his effort will be seen." Both refuse to call honest effort wasted.

teach.h: WHO SEES IT? AN HONEST DIFFERENCE.
teach.b: The honest difference is who sees it. The Qur'an goes on to say that effort will be repaid, and it is God who sees it. In the Buddhist texts there's no judge keeping count; the effort changes the mind doing it.
Two answers to why. One shared refusal to shrug.
Joyful effort: work that feeds the one who does it.

how: Many Buddhist teachers present effort as joyful rather than grim, often drawing on Shantideva's chapter on effort; in daily life it is practiced as doing ordinary tasks wholeheartedly and well.

games.q: what does “a day of effort” mean?
o: work you push through no matter how it hurts
a holiday when Buddhists rest from all work
steady effort with some delight in doing it

games.q: effort, two traditions — tap the pairs.
p: effort is delight in the good
that for which he maketh effort

s: in Buddhism, real effort should feel grim
Shantideva calls effort delight in the good.
the Qur'an says a person's effort will be seen
in Pickthall's words: "his effort will be seen."
Buddhist and Muslim texts say effort counts for the same reason
both say effort isn't wasted; they differ on who sees it and why.

games.q: your dad says his new gym routine only counts if he hates every minute. what would Shantideva say?
o: effort is delight in the good; enjoying it doesn't make it count less.
he's right: if it doesn't hurt, it isn't real effort.
skip the hard parts; effort should feel easy all the time.
games.why: Shantideva defines effort as delight in the good. joy keeps energy going; it doesn't cancel the work.

practice: Count three things you've done well lately with real effort, one on each finger: a dish properly washed, a hard message sent, a page finished.
For each, notice whether there's a small warmth in remembering it, and let that warmth stay.

wordCard.voice: A day of effort: steady work done with some delight in it, the way Shantideva defines effort.

orig.note: Sanskrit: effort, energy; Shantideva's word, the Pali viriya.

carryVoice: Here's the line: joyful effort, not grim and not frantic, just glad to be doing the good thing. Bye for now.

sources.ref: SN 46.53, Aggi Sutta (when the mind is sluggish, develop investigation, energy and rapture)
Shantideva, Bodhicaryavatara 7.2 (effort is delight in the good; laziness includes attachment to petty things and self-contempt)

sources.q: And that man hath only that for which he maketh effort, And that his effort will be seen.

sources.ref: Qur'an 53:41 (afterward he will be repaid for it)
